error_modes.label: Altitude control during descent and pattern entry

texts.0: SP, due to a late start of the descent out of the assigned flight area, did not achieve the altitude cleared by ATC before the VFR entry point. The formation arrived at the entry point more than 300 feet off the cleared altitude and the deviation was still increasing at the pattern entry. The IP intervened on the controls and re-established the formation on the cleared altitude before the break.
texts.1: SP, due to an unmonitored descent rate while handling lead duties, allowed the altitude to diverge from the cleared value up to the 300 feet limit. The divergence was arrested only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP, and the level-off was completed after the entry point instead of before it. SP did not use a lead point for the level-off and let the altimeter drive the correction.
texts.2: SP, due to a descent rate held slightly higher than required, let the altitude deviate about 200 feet from the value assigned by ATC, between the 150 and 300 feet limits. SP recognized the trend on the altimeter, reduced the rate and regained the cleared altitude in time for the entry point. No IP intervention was required and the deviation did not repeat.
texts.3: SP planned the descent from the flight area and held the cleared altitude within 150 feet throughout the return and the level-off, reaching the assigned altitude before the VFR entry point. Corrections were small, applied promptly and did not force power changes on the wingman.
texts.4: SP flew the descent and the level-off with altitude deviations that remained negligible against the cleared value, with the assigned altitude established well before the VFR entry point. The vertical profile was stable enough for the wingman to hold position with minimal corrections throughout the pattern entry.
texts.marginal: SP kept the altitude inside the required limits, but the deviations were consistently close to the upper part of the acceptable band and were corrected only after they had developed. The tendency was to chase the altimeter rather than to control the descent rate against a planned level-off point. SP is expected to anticipate the level-off and to reduce the size of the corrections in the next sorties.

texts_at.0: SP flew the descent and level-off with the lead point for the level-off talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first return and descent at this stage and anticipating the level-off point has not yet formed. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to anticipate the level-off point without the reminder on the next returns.
texts_at.1: SP held the descent with the altitude deviation reaching about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, because the level-off was completed only as the entry point arrived rather than anticipated in advance. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to anticipate the level-off point earlier so the deviation does not run to the edge of the tolerance.
texts_at.2: SP let the altitude deviate about 200 feet from the cleared value, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the descent rate reduction was made a beat after the trend was visible on the altimeter. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce the descent rate as soon as the trend appears rather than after it develops.
texts_at.3: SP held the cleared altitude within 150 feet through the return and the level-off on three of the four descents, the fourth needing a slightly larger correction after a level-off anticipated a little late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to anticipate every level-off with the same lead the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP led the descent and level off, holding the altitude deviation to about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, once the level-off was anticipated. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP caught the altitude trend developing toward 200 feet from the cleared value and reduced the descent rate without prompting, regaining the cleared altitude in time for the entry point. Reducing the descent rate as soon as the trend is seen, rather than after, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control on the descent.
texts_above.3: SP planned the descent from the flight area and held the cleared altitude within 150 feet throughout the return and the level-off, with corrections small, prompt and made without forcing power changes on the wingman. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude control on the descent.
texts_above.4: SP flew the descent and the level-off with altitude deviations that remained negligible against the cleared value, established well before the VFR entry point with a profile stable enough for the wingman to need minimal corrections. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude control on the descent.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control on the return and descent profile

texts.0: SP, due to an unadjusted power setting when the nose was lowered for the descent, allowed the airspeed to build beyond the briefed return speed by more than 20 knots. The excess speed compressed the time available for the pre-descent checks and left the wingman unable to hold position without excessive power. The IP took the controls and re-established the formation on the correct speed for the pattern entry.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed power reduction during the descent, let the airspeed deviate up to 20 knots from the value briefed for the return. The speed was restored only after verbal direction from the IP and the correction was applied abruptly, producing a further overshoot on the low side. SP did not cross-check the airspeed indicator against the descent rate.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting left slightly high at the top of the descent, allowed the airspeed to deviate about 15 knots, between the 10 and 20 knots limits. SP identified the deviation on the airspeed indicator, adjusted power smoothly and returned to the briefed speed before the entry point, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP held the airspeed within 10 knots of the value briefed for the return and descent, adjusting power in advance of the pitch changes. The speed was stable at the VFR entry point and gave the wingman a steady reference for the pattern entry.
texts.4: SP flew the whole return, descent and pattern entry with airspeed deviations that remained negligible, with power set ahead of every pitch change. The formation arrived at the entry point on the exact briefed speed and required no correction from the wingman.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed inside the required limits, but the value drifted continuously around the briefed figure and each correction produced a small overshoot in the opposite direction. The tendency was to react to the airspeed indicator rather than to set and trim a known power setting. SP is expected to stabilize the speed with a planned power setting and to reduce the frequency of the corrections.

texts_at.0: SP flew the return and descent with the cross-check between the airspeed indicator and the descent rate talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first return and descent at this stage and cross-checking the airspeed against the descent rate has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to cross-check the airspeed indicator against the descent rate without the reminder on the next returns.
texts_at.1: SP let the airspeed deviate about 20 knots from the value briefed for the return, at the tolerance limit, because the power reduction during the descent was made without a cross-check against the descent rate. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to cross-check the airspeed indicator against the descent rate so the correction is not left to the tolerance edge.
texts_at.2: SP let the airspeed deviate about 15 knots, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the power setting at the top of the descent was left slightly high before the trend was identified. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set the power correctly at the top of the descent rather than adjusting it once the trend is visible.
texts_at.3: SP held the airspeed within 10 knots of the briefed value on three of the four descents, the fourth needing a small correction after a power setting held a touch high. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to set the power on every descent as precisely as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP let the airspeed deviate about 20 knots from the value briefed for the return, at the tolerance limit, once the descent rate was cross-checked against the airspeed indicator. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP let the airspeed deviate toward 15 knots but identified it on the indicator and adjusted power smoothly without prompting, returning to the briefed speed before the entry point. Setting the power correctly at the top of the descent, rather than adjusting it once the trend is visible, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound speed control on the return and descent.
texts_above.3: SP held the airspeed within 10 knots of the value briefed for the return and descent, adjusting power in advance of the pitch changes so the speed was stable and gave the wingman a steady reference. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed speed control on the return and descent.
texts_above.4: SP flew the whole return, descent and pattern entry with airspeed deviations that remained negligible, power set ahead of every pitch change so the formation arrived on the exact briefed speed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional speed control on the return and descent.

error_modes.label: Heading accuracy to the VFR entry point

texts.0: SP, due to an inaccurate roll-out from the turn out of the flight area, established the formation on a heading more than 10 degrees off the one required for the authorized VFR entry point. The error was not detected on the heading indicator and the formation was displaced from the published entry track. The IP corrected the heading and repositioned the formation towards the entry point.
texts.1: SP, due to an anticipated roll-out combined with an incomplete heading cross-check, settled on a heading 10 degrees off the value required for the entry point. The heading was corrected only after the IP pointed out the error, and the roll back onto the correct track was late and abrupt for the wingman. SP did not confirm the roll-out heading before returning attention outside.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late roll-out from the turn towards the entry point, rolled out about 8 degrees off the required heading, between the 5 and 10 degrees limits. SP detected the error on the heading indicator immediately after roll-out and corrected it with a small smooth turn, without IP intervention and without disturbing the wingman.
texts.3: SP rolled out on the heading required for the authorized VFR entry point within 5 degrees on each turn of the return and pattern entry. Roll-outs were anticipated correctly, checked against the heading indicator and flown at a rate the wingman could follow.
texts.4: SP flew every turn of the return and pattern entry with heading errors that remained negligible at roll-out, tracking precisely towards the authorized VFR entry point. No corrective turns were needed after roll-out and the formation remained stable throughout.
texts.marginal: SP held the required headings inside the limits, but roll-outs were repeatedly a few degrees wide and were then closed with a second small turn. The tendency was to roll out late and correct afterwards rather than to anticipate the lead point. SP is expected to plan the roll-out and to arrive on the entry heading in one turn.

texts_at.0: SP rolled out toward the VFR entry point with the roll-out heading confirmation talked through by the IP before attention returned outside, because this is SP's first return to this pattern at this stage and confirming the roll-out heading before returning attention outside has not yet formed. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to confirm the roll-out heading before returning attention outside without the reminder on the next returns.
texts_at.1: SP settled on a heading about 10 degrees off the value required for the entry point, at the tolerance limit, because the heading was not confirmed before attention returned outside. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the roll-out heading before returning attention outside rather than after the correction is needed.
texts_at.2: SP rolled out about 7 degrees off the required heading, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the roll-out from the turn toward the entry point was anticipated a little late. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate that roll-out as early as the ones that hit the heading directly.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out within 5 degrees of the heading required for the entry point on three of the four turns, the fourth needing a small correction after a roll-out anticipated a fraction late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the same precision on every turn that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP settled on a heading about 10 degrees off the value required for the entry point, at the tolerance limit, once the heading was confirmed on the indicator. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP rolled out about 7 degrees off the required heading but detected the error on the heading indicator immediately and corrected it with a small smooth turn, without prompting and without disturbing the wingman. Anticipating the roll-out as early as the ones that hit the heading directly, rather than correcting it afterward, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid heading precision to the VFR entry point.
texts_above.3: SP rolled out on the heading required for the authorized VFR entry point within 5 degrees on each turn, with roll-outs anticipated correctly and checked against the heading indicator. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate heading precision to the VFR entry point.
texts_above.4: SP flew every turn of the return and pattern entry with heading errors that remained negligible at roll-out, tracking precisely toward the entry point with no corrective turns needed afterward. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding heading precision to the VFR entry point.

error_modes.label: Descent planning, pre-descent procedures and checks before the entry point

texts.0: SP, due to workload management that left the checklist unfinished before the descent, did not carry out the pre-descent procedures and checks and did not direct the formation in time towards the entry point. The formation arrived at the entry point without the required configuration and outside the cleared altitude by more than 300 feet. The IP took over the sequencing and completed the outstanding actions before the pattern entry.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the turn towards the entry point, started the pre-descent procedures late and completed them only after prompting from the IP. The formation reached the assigned altitude at the limit of the 300 feet band and the checks were finished after the entry point instead of before it.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly compressed descent plan, started the pre-descent checks later than briefed but reorganized the task sequence without prompting. The checks were completed before the entry point and the altitude deviation stayed between 150 and 300 feet, corrected in time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP directed the formation in time towards the entry point, carried out the pre-descent procedures and checks in the briefed sequence, and achieved the assigned altitude within 150 feet before the entry point. Radio, checks and formation direction were separated so that no task was left unfinished.
texts.4: SP planned and executed the return so that the pre-descent procedures and checks were complete well before the entry point, with the assigned altitude established early and the formation correctly positioned. Cockpit tasks were distributed across the descent with clear spare capacity for the ATC exchange and for the wingman.
texts.marginal: SP completed the pre-descent procedures and checks before the entry point, but with little margin and with the tasks bunched into the final part of the descent. The tendency was to begin the sequence only when the entry point became visible rather than at the planned point. SP is expected to start the descent sequence earlier and to spread the workload across the return.

texts_at.0: SP carried out the pre-descent procedures and checks with the sequencing talked through by the IP before the turn toward the entry point, because this is SP's first return at this stage and starting the pre-descent procedures before the turn toward the entry point has not yet formed. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to start the pre-descent procedures before the turn toward the entry point without the reminder on the next returns.
texts_at.1: SP reached the assigned altitude at about 300 feet from cleared, at the tolerance limit, because the pre-descent procedures were started only inside the turn toward the entry point and finished only after IP prompted. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to start the pre-descent procedures before the turn toward the entry point rather than inside it.
texts_at.2: SP started the pre-descent checks later than briefed but reorganized the task sequence without prompting, holding the altitude deviation to about 200 feet, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, corrected in time. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the checks at the briefed point rather than reorganizing the sequence after starting late.
texts_at.3: SP directed the formation in time and achieved the assigned altitude within 150 feet before the entry point on three of the four descents, the fourth needing a small correction after checks started a beat late. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to start the checks on every descent as promptly as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP reached the assigned altitude to about 300 feet from cleared, at the tolerance limit, once the pre-descent procedures were finished. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP started the pre-descent checks later than briefed but reorganized the task sequence without prompting, completing the checks before the entry point with the altitude deviation held to about 200 feet. Starting the checks at the briefed point, rather than reorganizing the sequence after starting late, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady sequencing of the pre-descent procedures.
texts_above.3: SP directed the formation in time towards the entry point, carried out the pre-descent procedures and checks in the briefed sequence and achieved the assigned altitude within 150 feet before the entry point, with radio, checks and direction kept separate. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined sequencing of the pre-descent procedures.
texts_above.4: SP planned and executed the return so the pre-descent procedures and checks were complete well before the entry point, with the assigned altitude established early and clear spare capacity for the ATC exchange and the wingman. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate sequencing of the pre-descent procedures.

error_modes.label: Use of VOR/DME, TACAN or GPS for orientation and return

texts.0: SP, due to navigation aids left unselected and unidentified after departure from the flight area, could not establish the position of the formation relative to the airport environment. The return track was flown on estimation only, the formation did not arrive at an authorized VFR entry point and the resulting heading error went beyond 10 degrees. The IP set up the navigation aid and directed the formation back towards the correct entry point.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete set-up of the VOR/DME, TACAN or GPS, used the available information only partially and remained uncertain about the distance to the entry point. Orientation with the airport environment was restored only after the IP identified the aid and pointed out the position, and the resulting heading error reached the 10 degrees limit.
texts.2: SP, due to a late selection of the required navigation aid, initially returned on visual reference alone and was slow to confirm the position of the formation. SP then identified the aid, cross-checked the bearing and distance and corrected the return track in time, with a heading error between 5 and 10 degrees and no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP selected and identified the VOR/DME, TACAN or GPS as required, remained oriented with the airport environment throughout the return and used the information to track towards the authorized VFR entry point within 5 degrees. Position and distance were cross-checked against the visual picture at each stage of the descent.
texts.4: SP used the navigation aids and the visual references together throughout the return, with position, distance and time to the entry point known at all stages and reported without hesitation. The orientation with the airport environment was continuous and the formation was placed exactly on the authorized entry point.
texts.marginal: SP used the navigation aids and remained oriented, but the information was consulted only at discrete moments and the position relative to the entry point was known with a delay. The tendency was to rely on the visual picture first and to confirm with the aid afterwards. SP is expected to keep a continuous cross-check between the aid and the visual references during the return.

texts_at.0: SP set up the navigation aid for the return with the selection and identification steps talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first return using this navigation aid at this stage and selecting the aid before relying on the visual picture has not yet formed. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to select and identify the required navigation aid without the reminder on the next returns.
texts_at.1: SP used the available navigation aid information only partially and remained uncertain about the distance to the entry point, with the resulting heading error reaching about 10 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before IP identified the aid and the position. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to select and identify the required navigation aid before relying on the visual picture alone.
texts_at.2: SP returned initially on visual reference alone and was slow to confirm the position, with the resulting heading error reaching about 7 degrees, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before the aid was identified and the return track corrected without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to select the navigation aid before the visual picture is relied on rather than after it proves insufficient.
texts_at.3: SP selected and identified the required navigation aid and tracked toward the entry point within 5 degrees on three of the four returns, the fourth needing a small correction after an aid identified a beat late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to identify that aid with the same promptness the first three returns showed.

texts_above.1: SP used the available navigation aid information, holding the resulting heading error to about 10 degrees, at the tolerance limit, once the aid was identified. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP returned initially on visual reference alone but then identified the aid, cross-checked bearing and distance and corrected the return track without prompting, holding the heading error to about 7 degrees. Selecting the navigation aid before relying on the visual picture, rather than after it proves insufficient, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured navigation aid cross-check on the return.
texts_above.3: SP selected and identified the required navigation aid, remained oriented with the airport environment throughout the return and tracked toward the entry point within 5 degrees, cross-checking position against the visual picture at each stage. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise navigation aid cross-check on the return.
texts_above.4: SP used the navigation aids and the visual references together throughout the return, with position, distance and time to the entry point known at all stages and the formation placed exactly on the authorized entry point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate navigation aid cross-check on the return.

error_modes.label: ATC compliance, read-back and awareness of entry points and approach procedure

texts.0: SP, due to an unstandard read-back that did not confirm the actual clearance, misapprehended the ATC directive for the return and flew the formation towards an entry point that had not been assigned. The error was not detected from the subsequent transmissions and the approach procedure was started from the wrong position. The IP took the radio and the controls and re-established the formation on the cleared routing.
texts.1: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous to the controller, received a clearance that was understood only in part and applied it late. The misapprehension about the assigned entry point was resolved only after the IP repeated the directive on the intercom, and the formation reached the entry point off the cleared parameters at the limits.
texts.2: SP, due to a read-back that omitted one element of the clearance, initially set an incorrect altitude for the entry, but requested confirmation from ATC on SP's own initiative. The clearance was clarified and complied with in time, the deviation stayed between the 150 and 300 feet limits and no IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP followed the ATC directives without misapprehension, read back the clearances in standard phraseology and remained cognizant of the assigned entry point and of the approach procedure in use. Every instruction was applied promptly and passed on to the wingman.
texts.4: SP handled the ATC exchange in standard phraseology with accurate and immediate read-backs, anticipated the routing to the assigned entry point and briefed the wingman on the approach procedure before it was required. Radio work remained concise and never competed with the flying task.
texts.marginal: SP complied with the ATC directives and remained cognizant of the entry point, but the read-backs were occasionally incomplete and one clearance required a second transmission to be confirmed. The tendency was to answer quickly rather than accurately under the workload of the descent. SP is expected to use standard phraseology and to read back the full clearance on every exchange.

texts_at.0: SP flew the ATC exchange for the return with the read-back and the assigned entry point talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first ATC exchange for this pattern at this stage and reading back the full clearance has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to read back the full clearance without the reminder on the next returns.
texts_at.1: SP reached the entry point with parameters about 300 feet off the cleared value, at the tolerance limit, because the misapprehension about the assigned point was resolved only after IP repeated the directive. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to read back the full clearance so a misapprehension is caught before it reaches the entry point.
texts_at.2: SP initially set an altitude about 200 feet off the cleared value after a read-back that omitted one element of the clearance, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before requesting confirmation from ATC without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to read back the complete clearance the first time rather than requesting confirmation after an element is omitted.
texts_at.3: SP followed the ATC directives and held the parameters within 150 feet on three of the four descents, the fourth read-back needing a second transmission to confirm one element. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to read back that one clearance as completely as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP reached the entry point with parameters about 300 feet off the cleared value, at the tolerance limit, once the misapprehension was resolved. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP initially set an altitude about 200 feet off the cleared value after an incomplete read-back but requested confirmation from ATC without prompting, complying with the clarified clearance in time. Reading back the complete clearance the first time, rather than requesting confirmation afterward, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent ATC compliance on the return.
texts_above.3: SP followed the ATC directives without misapprehension, read back the clearances in standard phraseology and remained cognizant of the assigned entry point and the approach procedure, applying every instruction promptly and passing it to the wingman. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed ATC compliance on the return.
texts_above.4: SP handled the ATC exchange in standard phraseology with accurate and immediate read-backs, anticipating the routing to the assigned entry point and briefing the wingman before it was required. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding ATC compliance on the return.

error_modes.label: Wingman positioning for the BREAK and direction of the formation to the active runway

texts.0: SP, due to an uncoordinated response between the two cockpits during the procedure, did not place the wingman on the side required for the BREAK and gave no direction towards the break of the active runway. The formation arrived at the initial with the wingman on the wrong side and outside the parameters for the pattern entry. The IP intervened, repositioned the formation and issued the required directions.
texts.1: SP, due to an unagreed division of duties within the formation, called the wingman to the BREAK side late and without confirming the new position. The wingman was still repositioning at the initial and the direction to the break of the active runway was given only after the IP prompted for it, with the entry parameters at their limits.
texts.2: SP, due to a signal to the wingman given later than briefed, started the repositioning for the BREAK behind the planned point, but recognized the delay and completed the change of side in time. The wingman was correctly placed and directed towards the break of the active runway before the initial, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP placed the wingman on the correct side for the BREAK at the planned point and directed the formation to the break of the active runway with clear and timely calls. The repositioning was flown steadily and the formation arrived at the initial correctly configured.
texts.4: SP placed the wingman on the BREAK side early and without ambiguity, kept the formation stable during the repositioning and directed it to the break of the active runway with concise calls that required no repetition. The whole sequence was flown so that the wingman needed no corrections at the initial.
texts.marginal: SP placed the wingman correctly for the BREAK and directed the formation to the active runway, but the calls came later than briefed and the repositioning was completed close to the initial. The tendency was to wait for the runway to become visible before acting rather than to use the briefed point. SP is expected to anticipate the repositioning and to give the direction calls earlier.

texts_at.0: SP positioned the wingman for the BREAK with the call to the BREAK side and the direction to the active runway talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first BREAK direction at this stage and calling the wingman to the BREAK side without a prompt has not yet formed. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to call the wingman to the BREAK side and direct the break of the runway without the reminder on the next returns.
texts_at.1: SP called the wingman to the BREAK side late and without confirming the new position, so the direction to the break of the active runway was given only after IP prompted for it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to call the wingman to the BREAK side and direct the break of the runway without needing the direction prompted.
texts_at.2: SP signalled the wingman to the BREAK side later than briefed, starting the repositioning behind the planned point, then recognized the delay and completed the change of side in time without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to signal the BREAK side at the briefed point rather than recognizing the delay afterward.
texts_at.3: SP placed the wingman on the correct side for the BREAK and directed the formation to the active runway at the planned point on three of the four approaches, the fourth call coming a moment later than ideal. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make that one call as promptly as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP called the wingman to the BREAK side and directed the break of the active runway once prompted for the direction. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP signalled the wingman to the BREAK side later than briefed but recognized the delay without prompting, completing the change of side and directing the formation to the active runway before the initial. Signalling the BREAK side at the briefed point, rather than recognizing the delay afterward, would remove that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable coordination of the wingman's BREAK position.
texts_above.3: SP placed the wingman on the correct side for the BREAK at the planned point and directed the formation to the break of the active runway with clear and timely calls, with the repositioning flown steadily. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good coordination of the wingman's BREAK position.
texts_above.4: SP placed the wingman on the BREAK side early and without ambiguity, keeping the formation stable during the repositioning and directing it to the active runway with concise calls that required no repetition. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior coordination of the wingman's BREAK position.

error_modes.label: Compliance with landing pattern procedures as described in LAPs

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete study of the Local Area Procedures, entered the traffic pattern from a point that is not a standard entry point and flew the pattern with altitudes and tracks that did not correspond to the published procedure. The deviations from the pattern altitude exceeded 300 feet and conflicted with the traffic sequence. The IP took the controls and re-established the formation on the published pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to an uncertain recall of the pattern altitudes and entry points described in the LAPs, entered the pattern at the correct point but with parameters at the 300 feet and 20 knots limits. The published profile was regained only after verbal direction from the IP and the pattern legs remained displaced from the described tracks.
texts.2: SP, due to a late identification of the standard entry point, joined the pattern slightly off the described track with an altitude deviation between the 150 and 300 feet limits. SP recognized the discrepancy against the LAP profile and corrected the entry in time, completing the pattern within the published procedure and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP entered the pattern from a standard entry point and followed the landing pattern procedures described in the LAPs, holding the pattern altitude within 150 feet and the pattern speed within 10 knots. The formation was integrated into the traffic sequence without any correction being required.
texts.4: SP flew the entry and the pattern exactly as described in the LAPs, with negligible deviations in altitude and speed and with the formation positioned correctly relative to the other traffic at every stage. The whole entry required no adjustment and left full capacity for lookout and radio.
texts.marginal: SP followed the landing pattern procedures within the published limits, but the tracks were flown wide of the described profile and the altitude was regained only after the entry point. The tendency was to reconstruct the procedure in flight rather than to fly it from prior preparation. SP is expected to review the LAP entry profile before the sortie and to fly the published tracks more precisely.

texts_at.0: SP entered the pattern with the standard entry point and the published profile talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first pattern entry at this stage and entering the pattern already matching the published profile has not yet formed. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to enter the pattern already matching the published profile without the reminder on the next entries.
texts_at.1: SP entered the pattern at the correct point but with parameters about 300 feet and 20 knots off the published profile, at the tolerance limit, before the profile was regained on IP's direction. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to enter the pattern already matching the published profile rather than regaining it after direction.
texts_at.2: SP joined the pattern slightly off the described track with an altitude deviation of about 200 feet, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before recognizing the discrepancy against the LAP profile and correcting the entry without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to identify the standard entry point before joining rather than correcting the entry after joining off track.
texts_at.3: SP entered from a standard entry point and held the pattern altitude within 150 feet and the pattern speed within 10 knots on three of the four entries, the fourth needing a small correction after an entry point identified a beat late. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to identify that one entry point as promptly as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP entered the pattern at the correct point, holding parameters to about 300 feet and 20 knots off the published profile, at the tolerance limit, once the profile was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP joined the pattern slightly off the described track but recognized the discrepancy against the LAP profile without prompting, correcting the entry and completing the pattern within the published procedure with the altitude held to about 200 feet. Identifying the standard entry point before joining, rather than correcting the entry afterward, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured compliance with the landing pattern procedure.
texts_above.3: SP entered the pattern from a standard entry point and followed the landing pattern procedures described in the LAPs, holding the pattern altitude within 150 feet and the pattern speed within 10 knots with no correction required. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise compliance with the landing pattern procedure.
texts_above.4: SP flew the entry and the pattern exactly as described in the LAPs, with negligible deviations in altitude and speed and the formation positioned correctly relative to other traffic at every stage. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate compliance with the landing pattern procedure.

error_modes.label: Radio calls at the proper location and reporting of actual location when deviating

texts.0: SP, flying as Number 1, transmitted the letdown and pattern entry calls at points other than the published reporting locations and never reported the actual location of the formation. ATC sequenced the formation on a position it had not reached, and the formation crossed the VFR entry point more than 300 feet off the cleared altitude while its own position was still being sorted out. The IP took the radios, reported the actual position and re-established the formation on the cleared profile.
texts.1: SP transmitted the entry call before reaching the proper location and, having departed from the published routing, gave no report of the actual position until the IP prompted for it. The correction was made verbally with the altitude at the 300 feet limit against the cleared value and the heading to the entry point at the 10 degrees limit. SP treated the call as an item to be discharged rather than as a position report.
texts.2: SP made one letdown call short of the published reporting point, recognized the error and immediately reported the actual location to ATC without prompting. The confusion cost about 200 feet against the cleared altitude before the descent profile was restored, and the deviation stayed inside the 300 feet limit and was removed before the entry point.
texts.3: SP made all letdown and entry calls at the proper locations, and where routing deviations occurred the actual position was reported at once. Altitude at the VFR entry point was held within 150 feet of the cleared value and the heading to the entry point within 5 degrees, with the ATC sequence never in doubt.
texts.4: SP made every radio call at the proper location, phrased so that ATC required no repetition, and reported any departure from the planned routing with the actual position before being asked. Altitude and heading at the VFR entry point showed negligible deviation and the wingman needed no repositioning as a result of the radio work.
texts.marginal: SP made the required calls and kept the formation inside limits, but two calls were transmitted on estimated rather than identified positions and the actual location was reported only once the discrepancy became obvious. The tendency is to fly the radio calls from the clock instead of from the ground reference. SP is expected to identify the reporting point visually before transmitting and to report the actual location whenever the formation is not where the call places it.

texts_at.0: SP made the letdown and entry calls with the actual-position report talked through by the IP whenever the routing departed from the call, because this is SP's first letdown at this stage and reporting the actual location whenever the formation departs from the routing has not yet formed. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to report the actual location whenever the formation departs from the routing without the reminder on the next letdowns.
texts_at.1: SP gave the correction verbally with the altitude at about 300 feet against the cleared value, at the tolerance limit, and the heading to the entry point at about 10 degrees, because the entry call was treated as an item to discharge rather than a position report. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to report the actual location whenever the formation departs from the routing the call implies, without needing the correction made verbally.
texts_at.2: SP made one letdown call short of the published reporting point, with the resulting altitude confusion costing about 200 feet, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before the actual location was reported to ATC without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to identify the reporting point visually before transmitting rather than after the confusion is recognized.
texts_at.3: SP made every letdown and entry call at the proper location and held the altitude at the entry point within 150 feet on three of the four returns, the fourth call needing the actual position reported after a small routing deviation. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the same accuracy on every call that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP reported the actual location, holding the altitude at about 300 feet against the cleared value, at the tolerance limit, and the heading to the entry point to about 10 degrees. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP made one letdown call short of the published reporting point but recognized the error and immediately reported the actual location without prompting, holding the resulting confusion to about 200 feet against the cleared altitude. Identifying the reporting point visually before transmitting, rather than after the confusion is recognized, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good radio position reporting on the letdown.
texts_above.3: SP made all letdown and entry calls at the proper locations, reporting the actual position at once wherever routing deviations occurred, and held the altitude at the entry point within 150 feet with the ATC sequence never in doubt. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good radio position reporting on the letdown.
texts_above.4: SP made every radio call at the proper location, phrased so ATC required no repetition, and reported any departure from the planned routing with the actual position before being asked. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent radio position reporting on the letdown.

error_modes.label: Estimation of pattern altitude winds instead of assuming the surface wind

texts.0: SP planned the letdown and the pattern entry on the reported surface wind and assumed it was the same as the wind at pattern altitude, using neither the crab required to hold the ground track nor the difference between GPS groundspeed and indicated airspeed. The formation was carried off the entry route and reached the entry point with the ground track more than 10 degrees off and the airspeed more than 20 knots off the planned letdown value. The IP took control, set the drift correction and repositioned the formation for the entry.
texts.1: SP carried the surface wind into the pattern altitude plan and applied no drift correction, so the formation drifted progressively off the planned ground track. The 60 to 1 rule was not used to estimate the crosswind component and the divergence was arrested only after repeated IP prompting, with the ground track at the 10 degrees limit at the entry point.
texts.2: SP flew the first part of the letdown on the surface wind and let the formation drift off the planned ground track, then compared GPS groundspeed with indicated airspeed, recognized the stronger wind at altitude and set a crab. The track error peaked between 5 and 10 degrees and was removed before the entry point without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP derived the wind at pattern altitude from the crab required to hold the ground track and from the difference between GPS groundspeed and indicated airspeed rather than assuming that the surface wind applied. Drift correction was set early and the formation held the entry route within 5 degrees of ground track and the planned letdown airspeed within 10 knots.
texts.4: SP evaluated the pattern wind before the letdown, cross-checked the ATIS surface wind against GPS groundspeed and against the crab actually required, and briefed the wingman on the crosswind expected in the pattern. Ground track and airspeed deviations along the entry route were negligible and the anticipated crosswind control requirement matched what was found at pattern altitude.
texts.marginal: SP set a drift correction and kept the entry route inside limits, but the first estimate was taken from the surface wind and the crab was refined only after the drift became visible against the ground. The trend is to accept the reported surface wind as the wind at pattern altitude. SP is expected to derive the pattern wind from groundspeed and crab before reaching the entry point.

texts_at.0: SP planned the letdown wind with the crab and the groundspeed comparison talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first time deriving the pattern-altitude wind at this stage and deriving the wind from groundspeed and crab has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to derive the pattern wind from groundspeed and crab without the reminder on the next letdowns.
texts_at.1: SP applied no drift correction and let the ground track diverge to about 10 degrees off, at the tolerance limit, because the 60 to 1 rule was not used to estimate the crosswind component until IP prompted repeatedly. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to derive the pattern wind from groundspeed and crab before the entry point rather than after repeated prompting.
texts_at.2: SP flew the first part of the letdown on the surface wind and let the ground track drift to about 7 degrees, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before comparing GPS groundspeed with indicated airspeed and setting a crab without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to compare groundspeed with indicated airspeed early in the letdown rather than after the drift is visible.
texts_at.3: SP derived the wind at pattern altitude from the crab required and held the entry route within 5 degrees of ground track on three of the four letdowns, the fourth needing a small correction after a crab set a beat late. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to set that one crab as early as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP let the ground track diverge to about 10 degrees off, at the tolerance limit, once the crosswind component was estimated. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP flew the first part of the letdown on the surface wind and let the ground track drift toward 7 degrees off, but compared GPS groundspeed with indicated airspeed and set a crab without prompting, removing the error before the entry point. Comparing groundspeed with indicated airspeed early in the letdown, rather than after the drift is visible, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound wind estimation for the pattern entry.
texts_above.3: SP derived the wind at pattern altitude from the crab required to hold the ground track and from the difference between GPS groundspeed and indicated airspeed, setting the drift correction early and holding the entry route within 5 degrees. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed wind estimation for the pattern entry.
texts_above.4: SP evaluated the pattern wind before the letdown, cross-checking ATIS against GPS groundspeed and the crab actually required, so ground track and airspeed deviations along the entry route were negligible. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional wind estimation for the pattern entry.

error_modes.label: Clearing turns during the VMC letdown for clearing, descent rate control and outside references

texts.0: SP flew the VMC letdown straight ahead with no clearing turns, kept the scan inside the cockpit on the instruments and did not clear the pattern entry route. The descent rate went unmonitored and the formation passed the cleared altitude by more than 300 feet with traffic on the entry route still unresolved. The IP intervened, levelled the formation and cleared the entry route.
texts.1: SP omitted the clearing turns during the VMC letdown, so the descent was flown on the vertical speed indicator alone with no outside reference for the rate and no clearing of the route ahead. The IP had to call for a clearing turn and then for the level-off, which was completed with the altitude at the 300 feet limit against the cleared value.
texts.2: SP began the letdown without clearing turns, but on realizing that the entry route ahead had not been cleared and that the descent rate was building, SP flew a clearing turn, regained the outside references and controlled the rate. The altitude deviation reached about 200 feet and was corrected before the entry point without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP used clearing turns during the VMC letdown to clear the pattern entry route, control the descent rate and keep the attention on outside visual references. The formation reached the cleared altitude before the entry point within 150 feet, and the wingman remained in sight throughout the turns.
texts.4: SP planned the clearing turns into the letdown so that clearing, rate control and outside references were all served without disturbing the wingman. Traffic was acquired visually well before the entry point and altitude and airspeed deviations during the descent were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP flew clearing turns and stayed inside limits, but the turns were placed where they were convenient rather than where the entry route needed clearing, and the descent rate was still controlled mainly from the instruments. The tendency is to treat the clearing turn as a formality. SP is expected to position the clearing turns against the intended entry route and to use the outside references to control the rate.

texts_at.0: SP flew the VMC letdown with the clearing turns talked through by the IP as the descent rate began to build, because this is SP's first VMC letdown at this stage and flying the clearing turn before the descent rate builds has not yet formed. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to fly the clearing turn during the letdown without the reminder on the next letdowns.
texts_at.1: SP had the level-off completed with the altitude at about 300 feet against the cleared value, at the tolerance limit, because the clearing turn and the level-off call both came only after IP prompted. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to fly the clearing turn during the letdown so the rate is controlled outside rather than by a prompted level-off.
texts_at.2: SP began the letdown without clearing turns and the altitude deviation reached about 200 feet, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before the entry route ahead was recognized as unclear and a clearing turn was flown without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fly the clearing turn before the descent rate builds rather than once the deviation is already visible.
texts_at.3: SP used clearing turns during the VMC letdown and reached the cleared altitude within 150 feet before the entry point on three of the four descents, the fourth needing a small correction after a clearing turn flown a beat late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to fly the clearing turn with the same timing on every descent that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP completed the level-off once the clearing turn was flown, holding the altitude to about 300 feet against the cleared value, at the tolerance limit. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP began the letdown without clearing turns but on recognizing the entry route ahead had not been cleared, flew a clearing turn without prompting, regaining the outside references and holding the altitude deviation to about 200 feet. Flying the clearing turn before the descent rate builds, rather than once the deviation is visible, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent clearing turn technique on the letdown.
texts_above.3: SP used clearing turns during the VMC letdown to clear the pattern entry route, control the descent rate and keep attention on outside references, reaching the cleared altitude before the entry point within 150 feet. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed clearing turn technique on the letdown.
texts_above.4: SP planned the clearing turns into the letdown so clearing, rate control and outside references were all served without disturbing the wingman, acquiring traffic well before the entry point with negligible deviations. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding clearing turn technique on the letdown.

error_modes.label: Low power settings below 20 % torque in the descent instead of speed brake
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, as Number 1, controlled the descent by reducing power well below 20 % torque instead of using the speed brake, leaving the wingman without the power range needed to hold position. Number 2 dropped out of position and the formation airspeed decayed more than 20 knots below the planned letdown value, so the entry point was crossed unstabilized. The IP took control, restored the power setting and used the speed brake to control the profile.
texts.1: SP repeatedly set power below 20 % torque during the descent instead of extending the speed brake, and the wingman was seen at idle and sliding aft. The IP had to call for power and for speed brake, and the airspeed reached the 20 knots limit below the planned letdown value before the profile was restored.
texts.2: SP initially reduced power below 20 % torque to hold the descent profile, but on seeing the wingman go to idle and begin to drift aft, SP restored the power setting and extended the speed brake. The airspeed loss was contained between 10 and 20 knots of the planned value and the formation was stabilized before the entry point without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP controlled the rate of descent with the speed brake rather than with low power settings and kept torque above 20 % throughout, so the wingman retained the power range needed for position keeping. The planned letdown airspeed was held within 10 knots and the altitude within 150 feet.
texts.4: SP planned the descent so that the speed brake did the work and torque never approached 20 %, giving the wingman a symmetric power range for the whole letdown. Airspeed and altitude deviations were negligible and the wingman held position with minimal throttle activity.
texts.marginal: SP kept the descent profile inside limits, but power was allowed to sit close to 20 % torque for long periods before the speed brake was used and the wingman was working the throttle near idle. The trend is to control the descent with power first and to reach for the speed brake only once the wingman is already struggling. SP is expected to use the speed brake as the primary rate control and to protect the wingman's power range.

texts_at.0: SP controlled the descent rate with power and the speed brake talked through by the IP as the primary rate control, because this is SP's first formation recovery descent at this stage and using the speed brake as the primary rate control has not yet formed. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to use the speed brake as the primary rate control without the reminder on the next descents.
texts_at.1: SP reached the entry point with the airspeed about 20 knots below the planned letdown value, at the tolerance limit, because power was repeatedly set below 20 percent torque instead of the speed brake being extended, until IP called for both. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to use the speed brake as the primary rate control so power never needs to be set below the minimum.
texts_at.2: SP initially reduced power below 20 percent torque and the airspeed loss reached about 15 knots below the planned value, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before restoring power and extending the speed brake without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to extend the speed brake as soon as the profile calls for extra drag rather than reducing power below the minimum first.
texts_at.3: SP controlled the descent with the speed brake and kept torque above 20 percent, holding the planned letdown airspeed within 10 knots on three of the four descents, the fourth needing a small correction after power sat close to the minimum. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold torque with the same margin on every descent that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP reached the entry point with the airspeed to about 20 knots below the planned letdown value, at the tolerance limit, once power and the speed brake were both applied. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP initially reduced power below 20 percent torque but on seeing the wingman go to idle, restored the power setting and extended the speed brake without prompting, containing the airspeed loss to about 15 knots below the planned value. Extending the speed brake as soon as the profile calls for extra drag, rather than reducing power below the minimum first, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady power management on the descent.
texts_above.3: SP controlled the rate of descent with the speed brake rather than with low power settings, keeping torque above 20 percent throughout so the wingman retained a usable power range, with the planned letdown airspeed held within 10 knots. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined power management on the descent.
texts_above.4: SP planned the descent so the speed brake did the work and torque never approached 20 percent, giving the wingman a symmetric power range for the whole letdown with negligible airspeed and altitude deviations. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate power management on the descent.

error_modes.label: Delay of power reduction until the turn at the Break point is initiated
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP reduced power on the run-in to the Break point instead of delaying the reduction until the turn was initiated, so the formation decelerated while still straight and level with the wingman in close. Airspeed at the Break was more than 20 knots below the planned value and the wingman overshot forward before the turn was started. The IP intervened on the power and re-established the run-in parameters.
texts.1: SP began the power reduction before the turn to the downwind was initiated and the run-in speed washed off ahead of the Break point. The IP had to call for power to be restored, and the Break was executed with the airspeed at the 20 knots limit below the planned value and the wingman correcting a forward overshoot.
texts.2: SP started to bring the power back slightly before initiating the turn at the Break point, recognized the deceleration and held the setting until the bank was established. The airspeed dropped between 10 and 20 knots below the planned value and was recovered before the wingman was displaced, with no IP intervention required.
texts.3: SP flew the run-in on speed and delayed the power reduction until the turn to the downwind was initiated, so the Break was smooth and the wingman was not pushed forward. Airspeed at the Break was within 10 knots of the planned value and the turn was flown at a constant rate.
texts.4: SP arrived at the Break point on speed, held the power until the bank was established and then reduced it smoothly, producing a Break that the wingman could time without correction. Airspeed and altitude deviations through the Break were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept the Break parameters inside limits, but the power came back a moment before the bank each time and the wingman had to check forward movement. The tendency is to anticipate the power reduction instead of keying it to the start of the turn. SP is expected to hold the power until the turn to downwind is initiated.

texts_at.0: SP flew the run-in to the Break with the timing of the power reduction talked through by the IP against the start of the turn, because this is SP's first Break at this stage and holding the power until the turn to downwind is initiated has not yet formed. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to hold the power until the turn to downwind is initiated without the reminder on the next Breaks.
texts_at.1: SP had the airspeed at the Break at about 20 knots below the planned value, at the tolerance limit, because power was reduced on the run-in before the turn was initiated and had to be restored on IP's call. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold the power until the turn to downwind is initiated rather than reducing it on the run-in.
texts_at.2: SP started to bring the power back slightly before initiating the turn at the Break point, and the airspeed dropped about 15 knots below the planned value, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before the setting was held until the bank was established without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to key the power reduction to the start of the turn rather than anticipating it slightly before.
texts_at.3: SP flew the run-in on speed and delayed the power reduction until the turn was initiated, holding the airspeed at the Break within 10 knots on three of the four Breaks, the fourth needing a small correction after a reduction started a moment early. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to key that one reduction as precisely as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP restored power on a verbal call, holding the airspeed at the Break to about 20 knots below the planned value, at the tolerance limit. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP started to bring the power back slightly before initiating the turn at the Break point but recognized the deceleration and held the setting until the bank was established without prompting, containing the airspeed loss to about 15 knots below the planned value. Keying the power reduction to the start of the turn, rather than anticipating it slightly before, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured timing of the power reduction at the Break.
texts_above.3: SP flew the run-in on speed and delayed the power reduction until the turn to the downwind was initiated, so the Break was smooth and the airspeed at the Break stayed within 10 knots of the planned value. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise timing of the power reduction at the Break.
texts_above.4: SP arrived at the Break point on speed, held the power until the bank was established and then reduced it smoothly, producing a Break the wingman could time without correction and negligible parameter deviation. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate timing of the power reduction at the Break.

error_modes.label: Echelon turns away from Number 2 once inside the VFR entry point
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, once established at pattern altitude inside the VFR entry point, turned into the wingman instead of flying the briefed echelon turns away from Number 2. Number 2 was forced to cross under unbriefed, lost the correct side for the Break, and the formation reached the initial more than 10 degrees off the required heading. The IP intervened, directed the wingman back to the briefed side and re-established the pattern entry.
texts.1: SP made the turns inside the entry point without regard to the wingman's side, so Number 2 had to reposition independently. The IP had to remind SP that all turns away from Number 2 are echelon unless briefed otherwise, and the heading at the initial reached the 10 degrees limit while the position was being sorted out.
texts.2: SP started one turn inside the entry point in the direction of the wingman, recognized that it should have been an echelon turn away from Number 2 and rolled out before the wingman was displaced. The heading error stayed between 5 and 10 degrees and the correct echelon geometry was restored before the initial without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP flew all turns inside the VFR entry point as echelon turns away from Number 2 as briefed, keeping the wingman on the outside and in sight. The formation held pattern altitude within 150 feet and arrived at the initial within 5 degrees of the required heading.
texts.4: SP managed the pattern entry so that every turn was an echelon turn away from the wingman, with each turn called before it was flown. Number 2 held position without repositioning and the altitude and heading deviations to the initial were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP flew the turns inside the entry point as echelon turns and stayed inside limits, but the calls came as the bank was going in and the wingman was left to react rather than to anticipate. The trend is to fly the geometry correctly without giving Number 2 any lead time. SP is expected to call each echelon turn before initiating it.

texts_at.0: SP flew the turns inside the VFR entry point with the echelon-away-from-Number-2 rule talked through by the IP before each turn, because this is SP's first pattern entry at this stage and flying every turn inside the entry point as an echelon turn has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to fly every turn inside the entry point as an echelon turn away from Number 2 without the reminder on the next entries.
texts_at.1: SP had the heading at the initial reach about 10 degrees off the required value, at the tolerance limit, because the turns inside the entry point were made without regard to the wingman's side until IP reminded that all such turns are echelon. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to fly every turn inside the entry point as an echelon turn away from Number 2 without needing the reminder.
texts_at.2: SP started one turn inside the entry point in the direction of the wingman, with the resulting heading error reaching about 7 degrees, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before recognizing that it should have been an echelon turn and rolling out before the wingman was displaced. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to recognize the echelon requirement before starting the turn rather than after it is under way.
texts_at.3: SP flew the turns inside the entry point as echelon turns away from Number 2 and held pattern altitude within 150 feet and heading within 5 degrees of the required value at the initial on three of the four entries, the fourth needing a small correction after a turn direction recognized a beat late. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to recognize that one turn direction as promptly as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP flew the turns as echelon once reminded that all turns away from Number 2 are echelon, holding the heading at the initial to about 10 degrees off the required value, at the tolerance limit. error_modes.label: Number 2 delay after the Break and spacing outside Number 1 ground track on downwind
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, flying as Number 2, started the turn to downwind less than the briefed minimum of 5 seconds after Number 1 executed the Break and did not position slightly outside Number 1's ground track. Spacing on downwind collapsed to the point that the pattern could not be continued, with SP more than 300 feet off pattern altitude while manoeuvring for separation. The IP took control and re-established the interval.
texts.1: SP counted the delay after Number 1's Break loosely and began the turn short of the 5 seconds minimum, rolling out inside Number 1's ground track. The IP had to direct an extension for spacing, and the resulting corrections took the airspeed to the 20 knots limit against the planned pattern value.
texts.2: SP started the downwind turn slightly early after the Break and initially settled inside Number 1's ground track, then recognized the closure and moved to the outside with a small extension. Spacing was restored before the perch point without IP intervention and pattern airspeed stayed within 20 knots of the planned value.
texts.3: SP waited the briefed minimum of 5 seconds after Number 1's Break, flew the turn to downwind and established the aircraft slightly outside Number 1's ground track. Spacing at the perch point was correct, pattern altitude was held within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 knots.
texts.4: SP timed the interval after the Break precisely, established the downwind slightly outside Number 1's ground track and arrived at the perch point with spacing that required no adjustment. Deviations in pattern altitude and airspeed were negligible throughout the pattern.
texts.marginal: SP respected the minimum delay after the Break and kept spacing inside limits, but the downwind was flown close to Number 1's ground track and the interval was maintained with throttle work rather than with geometry. The tendency is to fix the spacing late on downwind instead of setting it at the turn. SP is expected to establish the outside offset as the downwind is rolled out.

texts_at.0: SP flew the downwind turn after the Break with the minimum delay and the outside offset talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first time flying Number 2 in this pattern at this stage and establishing the outside offset as the turn is rolled out has not yet formed. texts_at.2: SP started the downwind turn slightly early after the Break and initially settled inside Number 1's ground track, with the resulting airspeed reaching about 15 knots against the planned value, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before moving to the outside with a small extension without prompting. texts_at.3: SP waited the briefed minimum delay and established slightly outside Number 1's ground track, holding pattern altitude within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 knots on three of the four downwinds, the fourth needing a small correction after an offset established a beat late. error_modes.label: Number 2 flying a normal pattern instead of following a poorly-flown pattern
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, flying as Number 2, followed Number 1's poorly-flown pattern instead of going around, accepting a perch point and a final turn that could not produce a stabilized approach. The approach was continued with the airspeed more than 20 knots off the planned value and the aircraft more than 300 feet off pattern altitude in the turn. The IP intervened and directed the go-around.
texts.1: SP recognized that Number 1's pattern was outside normal parameters but pressed on with it, moving the perch point to match instead of flying a normal contact pattern. The go-around was executed only after the IP directed it, with the pattern parameters already at the 300 feet and 20 knots limits.
texts.2: SP initially followed Number 1's wide and fast pattern, then judged that the perch point would not support a normal final turn and repositioned to the standard pattern parameters. The deviations peaked in the intermediate band and were corrected before the final turn without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP flew a normal contact pattern rather than copying Number 1's deviations, used the same perch point as briefed and held the pattern within 150 feet and 10 knots of the planned values. Where the leader's pattern would not have supported a safe approach, SP was ready to go around and said so.
texts.4: SP flew the pattern on its own parameters, held the briefed perch point with negligible deviation and stated the go-around criteria before the final turn. Number 1's pattern irregularities produced no corresponding error in SP's approach.
texts.marginal: SP kept the pattern inside limits but shaped it around Number 1's track, letting the perch point move with the leader instead of holding the normal contact pattern. The trend is to accept the leader's pattern as the standard. SP is expected to fly the briefed pattern parameters and to go around when the leader's pattern will not support a stabilized approach.
